## AI Agent Dev

### 2.2 Tool Use &amp; Environment Interaction

#### [Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins](<https://www.anthropic.com/research/ecdsa-curve-origins>)

Anthropic documents an LLM-assisted investigation that tested pseudorandom-generator hypotheses and recovered the origins of several standardized elliptic-curve seeds and base points. Its published verification code makes this a useful case study of combining model-generated hypotheses with exact computational checks in scientific investigation.

**Published:** 2026-10-16 · **First seen:** 2026-10-17T10:06:03.000Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Scientific Discovery, Tool Use, Verification

[Blog](<https://www.anthropic.com/research/ecdsa-curve-origins>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. The October 16 primary report explains generator scanning, hidden-state recovery, backward reconstruction and timestamp checks, and includes code and expected outputs for ten prime-curve seeds, four binary-curve seeds and six base points. Its stated sub-half-hour discovery is author-reported.

**Limitations:** A single investigation with an internal research model, not a controlled comparison or reusable agent-system evaluation. B-163 and several base-point origins remain unexplained; skipped candidate curves leave historical selection criteria uncertain. The result does not break ECDSA or demonstrate a weakness in the standardized curves. No independent reproduction.

## AI Training &amp; Inference Infra

### 3.3 Inference Engines &amp; Serving

#### [SGLang Powers Beam in Production](<https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-10-16-beam>)

SGLang integrates Beam's hybrid sliding-window and full-attention mixture-of-experts model with fused precision-sensitive operations and a jointly budgeted target-and-drafter cache for blockwise speculative decoding. The report explains how cache reuse, draft-memory placement and supported parallel layouts fit together for long-context agents, with public serving recipes and replay scripts that separate simulated acceptance from natural-workload measurements.

**Published:** 2026-10-16 · **First seen:** 2026-10-17T10:04:34.136Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Hybrid Attention, Speculative Decoding, KV Memory, Serving Recipes

[Blog](<https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-10-16-beam>) · [Code](<https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/tree/bench-openhands-gb300-sweep-beam/benchmark/beam_openhands>) · [Project](<https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Reflection/Beam-1_0>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. Read the full October 16 report, including target/draft cache placement, DFlash2 with attention data parallelism, heterogeneous TP transfer, precision/fusion gates and the reproduction appendix. The public benchmark branch, serving cookbook and PRs 40331/40492/40909 were retrieved. Beam has 501B total/23B active parameters, hybrid attention, FP32 routing and rounded scaled residuals. On four GB300 GPUs, the OpenHands NVFP4 TP4 replay uses 13 turns, about 74K initial tokens, about 220 output tokens per turn and approximately 92% prefix-cache hits; its 127.6K total token/s/GPU headline at concurrency 32 uses fixed simulated acceptance length four. The separate AgentX replay reports 83,504 total token/s/GPU and 43.9 P90 token/s/user at concurrency 96. These are distinct workloads, not an engine leaderboard.

**Limitations:** Total throughput includes cached input tokens and is not newly computed or output-token throughput. OpenHands uses simulated acceptance with real draft tokens, so it does not measure natural acceptance or model accuracy; AgentX has a different workload and latency percentile. Shared draft placement excludes HiCache, host retraction and DCP; private fallbacks and startup gates apply, and draft capture requires PP=1. BF16 and dynamic FP8 do not use the NVFP4 MegaMoE extension. TPU recipes are forthcoming. Production-API use is author-reported rather than independent reliability evidence. Miles training results are separate from serving quality, and no author code or model experiment was executed.

### 3.5 Kernels, Compilers &amp; Runtimes

#### [Hyper Optimizing Kimi K3 in vLLM: Moving Fast and Responsibly](<https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-16-kimi-k3-megakernel>)

This vLLM engineering report replaces Kimi K3's decode path with workload-tuned kernels that fuse projections, residual operations and GPU communication while overlapping expert computation and weight prefetch. It pairs measured decode gains with a scoped validation process for agent-written optimizations, showing how to accelerate supported Blackwell configurations without treating one synthetic benchmark as a general serving result.

**Published:** 2026-10-16 · **First seen:** 2026-10-17T10:02:23.261Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** GPU Kernels, Communication Fusion, GB300, Validation

[Blog](<https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-16-kimi-k3-megakernel>) · [Code](<https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61867>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. Read the complete dated Markdown and PR 61867 description, covering CuTe DSL projection/KDA kernels, DCP, NVLink fusion, sharded router work, expert overlap and weight prefetching. The blog reports no-speculation aggregate TP-group gains of 1.31-1.92x across TP8/16 and batch sizes 1-64 on GB300. Its 842 versus 488 decode token/s comparison uses synthetic DSpark acceptance length six and excludes prefill. The merged opt-in implementation includes task/numerical checks and investigation of a compiler load-before-wait bug. The contribution selected is the new detailed engineering report and validation evidence, not a first-ever code release: the PR opened October 15. The displayed blog date is October 16; its source was added October 17 01:21 UTC, which is source provenance rather than an asserted exact website publication time. Delayed discovery: the optimization work, scoped benchmarks and validation were already described in the October 15 PR, within this report's 72-hour discovery lookback and before its main window. This entry inspects the October 16 detailed blog on October 17; it does not claim the method or code first appeared in the main coverage window.

**Limitations:** Scope is GB300 TP8/TP16 within one NVLink domain; speculative batch coverage is narrower than the no-speculation batch-64 range. Synthetic acceptance and decode-only throughput do not establish normal serving speed. The AgentX 1.8x interactivity comparison uses 16 optimized GPUs versus eight earlier GPUs. Blog and PR use different benchmark snapshots. Task scores near one standard error and sensitive long-context checks are not bitwise equivalence or general production reliability proofs. Development and review savings are not quantified. No independent reproduction was performed. The PR predates the main window, so the dated blog does not reset the optimization's age; inclusion is explicitly a delayed discovery, not an indexing-delay claim.
